concepts.name: Major groups of microbes
concepts.summary: Name and distinguish bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, protozoa and algae by basic features such as size, cellular organisation and examples.

concepts.name: Prokaryotic cell structure
concepts.summary: Describe the bacterial cell envelope, nucleoid, ribosomes, flagella and pili and explain what each does.

concepts.name: Bacterial binary fission
concepts.summary: Explain how bacteria divide by binary fission and why populations can grow exponentially.

concepts.name: Virus structure and nature
concepts.summary: Describe a virion as a nucleic acid genome in a protein capsid, sometimes enveloped, and explain why viruses need host cells to replicate.

concepts.name: Microscopy and staining basics
concepts.summary: Explain how light microscopy, simple staining and magnification reveal microbes.

concepts.name: Gram stain differences
concepts.summary: Explain how Gram-positive and Gram-negative walls differ and why this produces different staining results.

concepts.name: Beneficial and harmful microbes
concepts.summary: Give examples of microbes that cause disease and others that aid digestion, food production and nutrient cycling.

concepts.name: Sterile technique principles
concepts.summary: Explain why contamination matters and how aseptic handling prevents it.

misconceptions.text: All bacteria are harmful germs that cause disease.
Viruses are just very small bacteria.
Gram-positive bacteria are those that cause disease, and Gram-negative ones are harmless.

concepts.name: Bacterial growth curve phases
concepts.summary: Interpret a growth curve and identify lag, exponential, stationary and death phases and what drives each.

concepts.name: Environmental growth requirements
concepts.summary: Classify microbes by oxygen, temperature, pH and salt needs and predict where they can grow.

concepts.name: Energy and carbon nutritional types
concepts.summary: Classify organisms by energy and carbon source.

concepts.name: Culture media types
concepts.summary: Choose among defined, complex, selective, differential and enriched media to grow or identify an organism.

concepts.name: Isolation by streak plating
concepts.summary: Use streaking and dilution to obtain isolated colonies and count them as colony forming units.

concepts.name: Fermentation versus respiration
concepts.summary: Compare aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation in ATP yield and end products.

concepts.name: Viral replication cycle
concepts.summary: Apply the steps of attachment, entry, synthesis, assembly and release and contrast lytic with lysogenic cycles.

concepts.name: Physical and chemical microbial control
concepts.summary: Select heat, filtration, radiation, disinfectants or antiseptics for a given situation and distinguish sterilisation from disinfection.

misconceptions.text: Counting colonies on a plate gives the total number of cells, living and dead, in the sample.
Anaerobes are killed by any trace of oxygen and all non-aerobes behave the same way.
Disinfection and sterilisation mean the same thing.

concepts.name: Bacterial genome organisation
concepts.summary: Describe circular chromosomes, plasmids, operons and how they differ from eukaryotic genomes.

concepts.name: Operon gene regulation
concepts.summary: Analyse how repressors, inducers and catabolite repression control lac and trp operon expression under different conditions.

concepts.name: Horizontal gene transfer
concepts.summary: Distinguish the three mechanisms and analyse how each spreads traits like resistance.

concepts.name: Antimicrobial mechanisms of action
concepts.summary: Match antibiotic classes to targets such as cell wall, ribosome, folate synthesis and DNA replication, and explain selective toxicity.

concepts.name: Antibiotic resistance mechanisms
concepts.summary: Analyse how enzymatic inactivation, target modification, efflux and reduced uptake produce resistance and how selection spreads it.

concepts.name: Pathogenesis and virulence factors
concepts.summary: Analyse how adhesins, toxins, capsules and invasion factors contribute to infection, including exotoxin versus endotoxin.

concepts.name: Innate and adaptive host defence
concepts.summary: Apply knowledge of barriers, phagocytes, antibodies and T cells to explain responses to bacterial and viral infection.

concepts.name: Susceptibility testing
concepts.summary: Interpret minimum inhibitory concentration and zone of inhibition results.

misconceptions.text: Antibiotics create resistance in individual bacteria that then adapt in response to the drug.
Antibiotics are effective against viral infections such as colds.
A larger zone of inhibition always means a drug is better, regardless of the drug or organism.

concepts.name: Biofilm formation and tolerance
concepts.summary: Analyse how biofilm development, quorum sensing and matrix protection raise tolerance to antimicrobials and host defences.

concepts.name: Epidemiology of infectious disease
concepts.summary: Analyse transmission routes, reservoirs, R0 and herd immunity to interpret outbreak data.

concepts.name: Molecular diagnostic methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate culture, PCR, antigen, serological and sequencing methods for sensitivity, specificity and speed in a clinical scenario.

concepts.name: Viral evolution and immune escape
concepts.summary: Analyse how mutation, reassortment and recombination drive variants and affect vaccine and drug strategies.

concepts.name: Vaccine design strategies
concepts.summary: Evaluate live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, conjugate and nucleic acid vaccines for safety and immune response.

concepts.name: Microbiome and host interaction
concepts.summary: Analyse how commensals provide colonisation resistance and how dysbiosis or antibiotics contribute to disease.

concepts.name: Microbial ecology and biogeochemical cycles
concepts.summary: Analyse the microbial roles in nitrogen, carbon and sulfur cycles and in wastewater treatment.

concepts.name: Antimicrobial stewardship evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate treatment choices and policies to balance cure against selection of resistance.

misconceptions.text: A positive PCR result always means a viable, infectious organism is present.
Herd immunity requires everyone to be immune to protect the population.
Antibiotic courses should always be extended to prevent resistance, regardless of the infection.

concepts.name: Comparative genomics and phylogeny
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence from genome comparison, pan-genomes and phylogenies to infer evolution, outbreak linkage and gene transfer.

concepts.name: Metagenomic study design
concepts.summary: Design metagenomic or amplicon studies, controlling for bias and contamination, to characterise uncultured communities.

concepts.name: Genetic engineering of microbes
concepts.summary: Design engineered strains or pathways using plasmids and genome editing, including biocontainment considerations.

concepts.name: Novel antimicrobial strategy design
concepts.summary: Create approaches such as phage therapy, anti-virulence agents or combination regimens, justified by mechanism and resistance risk.

concepts.name: Evaluating causation in infection
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a microbe causes a disease using Koch's postulates and their molecular and metagenomic extensions.

concepts.name: Host-pathogen coevolution
concepts.summary: Evaluate trade-off models of virulence and transmission and how host and pathogen adapt to each other.

concepts.name: Biosafety and risk assessment
concepts.summary: Judge biosafety levels, containment and dual-use risk for work with specific agents.

concepts.name: Experimental design in microbiology
concepts.summary: Design controlled, reproducible experiments and critique published microbiological evidence.

misconceptions.text: Virulent pathogens inevitably evolve to become harmless over time.
Detecting a microbe's DNA in diseased tissue proves it caused the disease.
Relative abundance from sequencing reflects the true absolute abundance of organisms in a sample.
